title: Conditioning polymer clay for a smooth finish
subtitle: How to warm, work, and prepare polymer clay before use
excerpt: Polymer clay straight from the packet is stiff and may crack if bent. Conditioning softens the clay, distributes plasticisers evenly, and removes air pockets before forming. Properly conditioned clay produces smoother, stronger finished pieces with fewer cracks during curing.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from standard polymer clay practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working raw polymer clay by hand or roller until it is uniformly soft, pliable, and free of air pockets

content.text: is the most common cause of cracks in cured polymer clay pieces. The goal is to warm the clay to a uniform softness and eliminate any stiff cores or hard seams that would create weak points when cured. The process takes 2 to 5 minutes per 50 g of clay.

If the clay is very stiff, warm it briefly before working. Hold the block in your hands for 2 to 3 minutes, or place it in a sealed bag and submerge in warm (not hot) water for 5 minutes. Do not put raw clay in the oven to soften: partial curing will ruin it.
Once the clay gives when pressed, slice it into thin sheets with a fettling knife (approximately 5 mm thick) and stack the slices.
Roll the stack flat with the rolling pin to about 5 mm thick. Fold the slab in half, then roll flat again. Rotate 90 degrees and repeat.
Continue folding and rolling for 15 to 20 passes. The clay is conditioned when it can be bent double without cracking at the fold.
If small air bubbles appear as a rough texture on the rolled surface, fold and roll slightly more. Persistent bubbles can be pierced with a needle tool and pressed flat.

Roll a log of conditioned clay and bend it into a U shape. No cracks at the fold means the clay is ready. Conditioned clay not needed immediately can be wrapped tightly in cling film and stored at room temperature, away from heat and direct sunlight.

items.problem: Clay crumbles or tears into pieces when rolled rather than flattening
items.cause: The clay is very old or has been stored in a very cold environment and the plasticisers have partly separated
items.fix: Crumble the clay and add a tiny amount of petroleum jelly (about 1 g per 50 g of clay). Knead by hand until mixed in, then try conditioning again.

items.problem: Clay is very sticky and sticks to the work surface
items.cause: The room is warm or the clay was over-warmed before conditioning, making it too soft
items.fix: Rest the clay on a cool ceramic tile for 5 minutes before continuing. Work in a cooler area if possible. Refrigerate for 10 minutes as a last resort
